newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Waigel maps out budget plans for EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Waigel maps out budget plans for EMU.

text.p: The German government approved budget packages on Friday for this year and next that sharply raise the 1997 deficit and which Finance Minister Theo Waigel said set the stage for German entry to European monetary union.

Stuck in a phase of economic growth too feeble to create jobs, Germany has seen tax revenues falling and unemployment soaring to record levels, forcing Waigel to resort to selling off state assets and even the country's oil reserves in his bid to fit Germany into the Maastricht straitjacket.

But after weeks of horse-trading with federal ministers on spending limits, the wily Bavarian told reporters a special budget for 1997 ensured Germany would meet fiscal targets for monetary union and in 1998 things could only get better.

"The total public deficit will be 110 billion marks in 1997. Based on this, Germany will fulfil the deficit criterion in the Maastricht Treaty," Waigel said. "The current projection is for 3.0 percent. In 1998 it will be considerably lower."

Countries hoping to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 will be judged by economic performance in 1997 and they must meet fiscal targets, the most important being a limit on public deficits to three percent of economic output.

A debate is raging in Germany over whether the somewhat vague wording of the treaty means a country must hit 3.0 on the nose, or whether a slight overshooting is allowed if mid-term financial planning shows a trend toward budget stability.

The issue could be crucial when the time comes next year to deciding who will join the first wave of monetary union, because France -- which together with Germany is a key driver of European integration -- risks missing the deficit target.

Waigel's special budget for 1997 allows the federal deficit to balloon to 71.2 billion marks ($40.6 billion), up 17.9 percent from the original plan of 53.3 billion. Federal spending rises slightly to 458.6 billion marks from 455.6 billion in 1996.

The 1998 draft budget pegs the deficit at 57.8 billion marks, which is forecast to fall to 47 billion by 2001. Federal spending will rise to 461 billion marks next year and further to 480 billion marks in 2001.
Waigel predicted the economy would grow around 2.5 percent this year and 2.75 percent next year, with growth easing back to 2.5 percent in each of the three years following.
Although the government is confident it can still qualify for monetary union, independent economnists seem doubtful.

"Germany's deficit plans for the next 18 months do not inspire confidence," said Stephen King, an economist with James Capel in London, in a report. "In underlying terms, the federal accounts provide no real guarantees that Germany will meet the Maastricht deficit criterion either this year or, indeed, next."
Ros Lifton, economist at HSBC Markets, said in a report that the budget showed that German public finances remained in poor shape despite the recovery in the manufacturing sector.
"The upward revision to the 1997 federal deficit is bound to reinvigorate the by now familiar mantra that Germany will fail to meet the Maastricht deficit criterion," she said.

Waigel said stepped-up privatisations such as of phone giant Deutsche Telekom and Lufthansa airline, plus a surplus in the social security system, would help Germany meet the deficit target, but admitted the government left little room for error. "There is no reserve built into the 1997 deficit," he said.
The new budget did not account for tax cuts next year and there was still no deal in parliament on plans to lower tax by 30 billion marks over the next two years.

Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, finance expert for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said Waigel's budget mis-argeted cost cuts and would do little to create jobs for the more than four million Germans out of work.
She also said it was too early to predict whether Germany would meet the Maastricht deficit target. She added, however, that target need not be interpreted strictly.
"If the mark can be stable with 3.1 percent, then the euro can as well," she told a news conference. ($ = 1.753 German Marks)
